titleZh: 没有天然温泉，酒店能靠「碳酸泉」做出差异化招牌吗？
titleEn: Can a Hotel Without a Natural Hot Spring Build a Signature “Carbonated Spring” Experience?
summaryZh: 不依赖天然泉源，人工高浓度碳酸浴也能让酒店拥有可命名、可测量、可复制的水体验招牌。本文给出两类酒店与三类场景的选择方法、工程运营硬条件与单店试点纪律；公开案例只证模式，不证增收。
summaryEn: Without a natural spring, an artificial high-concentration carbonated bath can still give a hotel a nameable, measurable and replicable signature water experience. This article sets out scenario choices across two hotel types and three settings, engineering and operating preconditions, and a single-hotel pilot discipline; public cases support the model, not revenue claims.
contentZh:
没有天然温泉，酒店能靠「碳酸泉」做出差异化招牌吗？

能，但有前提。人工高浓度碳酸浴不依赖天然泉源，却能让酒店获得一个可命名、可测量、可标准化复制的水体验。真正决定这笔投入是否成立的，不是设备本身，而是场景选择、通风与浓度运维、宣传口径合规，以及先试点再测算的纪律。本文面向酒店投资者与业主，讲清它是什么、落在哪里、怎样用最小范围的试点验证需求，而不是凭行业案例直接下投资结论。

先厘清一个前提：人工碳酸浴不是天然温泉

行业里常听到的「碳酸泉」「人工碳酸泉」「碳酸浴」「气泡浴」，指的多是同一类人造溶气浴。为与天然温泉、天然碳酸泉严格区分，本文统一称人工高浓度碳酸浴。它依靠溶气或混合设备，把符合相关规范的食品级二氧化碳均匀溶入循环或静置浴水；客人能感受到细密气泡附着皮肤、水温不必很高却有回暖感、以及弱酸性肤感。这些都是体验现象，适合用来设计到店体验，本身不等于医疗功效的证明。

浓度是这个产品少有的可量化锚点。业界对外沟通时常以游离二氧化碳约不低于1000ppm作为高浓度叙事口径，日本口径为每千克1000毫克，在稀溶液中约等于1000ppm，源自日本疗养泉相关判定讨论中的浓度门槛之一。稳妥的标注方式是写明「约不低于1000ppm，参照日本疗养泉标准语境」。需要如实说明的是，人造浴水不属于日本《温泉法》意义上的温泉，不能称为疗养泉，也不意味着按中国法规它属于温泉。酒店宜自备检测手段、留存抽检记录，对外用注明时间与方法的实测数据说话，比堆砌形容词更可信。

它与天然泉的边界必须划清。天然碳酸泉来自地质泉源，稀缺且受地理约束，卖点是成分检测与产地故事；人工高浓度碳酸浴来自设备溶气，可复制、城市酒店也能用，卖点是浓度可控、气泡可视、体验标准化。两者可以同店并存，但要分池、分话术、分物料；有泉酒店引入人工产品，物料上应写明人工补充体验，不能写成「同样的天然碳酸泉」。益处表达同样有边界：所有体验描述都不是医疗结论，不保证个体效果，也不构成治疗建议，酒店物料不应出现承诺医学结果的表达，「血行促进」等容易被读成医疗承诺的词也应慎用，优先使用温暖感、放松感的表达。

它回应的是酒店差异化的四个投资条件

站在投资者角度，一个值得做的体验项目应同时满足四条：可复制，不依赖稀缺自然资源，门店之间能标准复制；可命名，能写进房型名称、预订页面和会员套餐；可测量，关键指标可以检测留痕，宣传有实据；可小步验证，允许先做小规模试点，再用真实数据决定投入节奏。人工高浓度碳酸浴恰好同时符合这四条。

它给经营侧提供的是几条可以设计、也可以观察的路径，而不是任何增收承诺。一是品质差异化与定价逻辑，在同城无泉或同质化供给中增加能拍照、能解释的体验卖点，为房型或套餐撑起价值叙事；二是房型结构优化，私汤房型或主题房把部分标准房升级为体验型供给；三是复购与口碑，气泡与回暖感容易沉淀为点评关键词，要观察的是客人会不会主动提及，而非预设好评率目标；四是淡旺季填充，商务淡季用放松过夜场景做主题推广；五是非房收入，SPA汤屋、双人泡池时段与体验区加购构成客房之外的体验动线，能否成立取决于动线与人力。这些都是逻辑路径，不是已验证的财务结论，具体价差与测算必须回到单店数据。

落在哪里：两类酒店与三类场景的选择

投资成败的第一步不是选设备，而是选对第一个场景。可选范围聚焦客房、SPA与泳池三类酒店内场景，不涉及公共大浴场。

无泉源的城市商务酒店，首期建议以客房浴缸加装为主，条件允许再配SPA汤屋为辅，泳池优先做旁侧体验区，整池溶气不作为首期默认项。浴缸加装改动聚焦，适合先在行政楼层或主题房挑几间试点，硬条件是浴室通风、浓度与气源管理、入浴提示卡三样先到位；私汤房型适合做成招牌房，能拍照、能写进房型名和相册，前提是防水、排水、隔音与运维流程先想清楚。SPA私密汤屋和双人泡池适合承接周末情侣与商务招待，没有SPA楼层的纯商务店可以暂缓，体验只做一半反而伤口碑。

已有温泉或康养设施的度假酒店，首期建议以私汤房型或SPA私密汤屋为主，泳池旁侧体验区为辅；真泉大池保持原有叙事，人工产品一律明确标出人工二字。客房和私汤承担的是客人不想去大池时的私密选项，或是天气与高峰时段的分流，而不是改写真泉的故事；任何物料都禁止出现与天然碳酸泉同一功效之类的表述。

泳池有两个方案。方案甲是整池溶气，只有完成专项评估后才能考虑，评估至少覆盖五件事：水面二氧化碳逸出、室内空气质量与通风换气、酸碱度与消毒体系的兼容性、低温体感与客人预期的差异、救生与开放时段管理，评估完成前不对外宣传泳池也是碳酸浴。方案乙是旁侧体验区，用独立小池或体验槽承接体验，循环和浓度更好控制，既是可视化打卡点，也是家庭客与商务客的轻量入口，适合作为多数酒店的泳池首选。无论从哪个场景起步，物料都要写清名称、建议浸泡时长区间、通风提示与禁忌摘要，画面优先拍气泡附着和浓度说明牌，而不是空泛的形容词海报。

同一套设施，五类客群各有入口

一套设施可以在不同时段、通过不同渠道承接五类客群，且没有主次之分。高净值银发康养客群看重私密、节奏慢与清晰的安全提示，适配私汤房型与SPA汤屋，通过康养自媒体、线下社区机构与体检后的兴趣触达沟通，定位是康养兴趣而非诊疗。社会高档消费客群为仪式感和独特体验付费，适配汤屋、景观泡池与主题套房，触达靠品牌官网、高端社群与质感短视频。高级商务客群需要差旅后房内即可完成的快速放松，适配浴缸加装与行政楼层房型，走协议公司、OTA商务筛选与前台管家话术。情侣客群要双人私密与纪念感，适配双人泡池与私汤房，适合短视频、周末套餐与纪念日主题。高消费家庭看重亲子放松与安全可控，旁侧体验区比整池更易控，走家庭套餐、本地生活与会员活动。

医院、体检与保健部门只用于兴趣触达：可以向关注生活方式的人群传递体验信息，但不做医院推荐、医生背书、联名诊疗，不与具体诊疗项目做对照，不把体检报告与任何效果承诺绑定，也不做任何暗示医学适应的表达。

工程与运营：决定成败的硬条件

设备侧不绑定任何品牌，业主可按五个模块自主比选供应商。溶气与混合设备看能否稳定达到约定浓度区间，以及噪音与占地；气源与管路看气瓶合规存放、泄漏监测与更换动线；水处理与循环要看是否和现有消毒、酸碱度体系冲突；通风与空气质量看换气次数、报警或巡检制度；监测模块要看浓度抽检与水温记录能否由非专业员工执行。

不同场景的安装要点不同。客房浴缸先做单房或几间试点，盯住浴室排风与提示卡；私汤房型的土建防水和排水优先于设备型号，并预留维修空间；SPA汤屋用预约制更利于浓度控制与清洁周转；泳池整池必须由机电、水处理、暖通与安全多方联合评估；旁侧体验区优先独立循环，避免拖垮主泳池的水质模型。

日常运营有五个关键动作：前台与管家话术统一为人工高浓度碳酸浴、放松体验、非医疗；入浴提示卡写清时长、通风、禁忌与应急呼叫方式；日常检查覆盖浓度抽检、通风、气源余量与水质指标；新员工上岗前完成话术与应急演练；客诉规则提前定好，退换或改期不以效果式承诺安抚。禁忌提示须结合当地规范与法务审定，至少覆盖饮酒后、急性疾病期、严重心肺等疾病人群慎用或遵医嘱、高龄及行动不便者勿独自入浴、儿童须有监护、孕妇等特殊人群按医嘱与店内政策处理。

公开案例能证明什么，不能证明什么

公开资料能够核验的，是设施存在与否、官方是否将其作为卖点、运营模式是否可查，几乎找不到可复核的增收比例。

日本商务连锁Super Hotel的官方门店页把高浓度人工炭酸泉列为魅力点，部分门店以命名汤强化记忆，值得借鉴的是它把设施写进预订决策信息，而不是藏在设施介绍末页；但日本市场与国内法规、客群、房价体系不同，没有公开可复核的增收比例，其公共浴场形态只作行业参照，并不意味着建议国内酒店做公共大浴场。台湾傑仕堡有氧酒店等城市酒店把人工碳酸泉汤屋与楼层SPA组合，启发在于用楼层SPA承接加购与停留延长，个案的地理与客群条件不能直接复制为财务模型。国内已有酒店与会所通过供应商落地同类设施，这类信息只作供应商线索，决策前应实地考察、合同核验，不把厂商宣传当作创收依据。阳宗海、漱心峡谷等天然碳酸泉度假地代表的是稀缺真泉叙事，人工路线不应借名，而要讲浓度可控、体验标准、城市可用的另一个故事。一句话，学模式，不学数字。

先试点再测算：把判断交给单店数据

最稳妥的路径分四步：场景选型，在矩阵中圈格；小范围试点，数间房型或汤屋，或一个体验区；观察项记录；单店测算与面谈。试点范围建议只选一格或两格，周期30到60天，首期不追求全场景铺开；涉及具体投入与财务测算的部分，结合单店条件在试点后另行沟通。

试点只做观察，不预设目标数值。曝光层看设施页点击、相册停留与短视频评论关键词；转化层看主题房预订占比、体验加购次数与到店升级接受度；价值叙事层看是否出现客户愿意接受的房型差价成交，而不预设具体数值；口碑层看点评与问卷是否主动提及气泡、回暖、放松；运营层看浓度达标率、通风与气源异常、客诉类型与员工执行难度；体验层看满意度开放题，不适与禁忌相关事件作为归零容忍项单独统计。节奏上先用一周由工程、市场、客房共同圈定场景，再用一周完成安装与话术过关，随后进入以周为单位的观察期，最后复盘面谈，指定一名客房或SPA经理作为负责人，每周只交一页观察表。

也要同时设定不适用与停止条件。解决不了通风与气源安全的客房、指望装上就成医疗康养标杆的定位、想把公共大浴场当首推路径却没有相应运营能力、希望通过医院合作输出医学背书，这四种情形应在决策阶段排除。试点期成交增量不为正、客人预订选择无变化、运维成本高于预期，或出现无法闭环的客诉与安全风险，就应暂停并复盘，不因投入已经发生而继续追加。

设施存在不等于需求与收益已经验证。人工高浓度碳酸浴给酒店的不是一张医学证书，而是一套可以复制的体验差异化工具：无泉城市借它做招牌，有泉度假用它补私密、承分流。先试点，再测算，单店验证之后再谈扩大，这才是对投资者最稳妥的顺序。
contentEn:
Can a Hotel Without a Natural Hot Spring Build a Signature “Carbonated Spring” Experience?

Yes, with conditions. An artificial high-concentration carbonated bath does not rely on a natural spring source, yet it can give a hotel a water experience that is nameable, measurable and standardised enough to replicate. What decides whether the investment holds is not the equipment itself, but scenario selection, ventilation and concentration management, compliant messaging, and the discipline of piloting before any financial calculation. Written for hotel investors and owners, this article explains what the product is, where it belongs, and how a smallest-viable pilot can test demand, rather than drawing investment conclusions straight from industry cases.

First, a premise: an artificial carbonated bath is not a natural hot spring

The terms often heard in the market, including “carbonated spring”, “artificial carbonated spring”, “carbonated bath” and “bubble bath”, mostly refer to the same family of manufactured gas-dissolving baths. To keep a strict line from natural hot springs and natural carbonated springs, this article consistently uses the term artificial high-concentration carbonated bath. It uses gas-dissolving or mixing equipment to diffuse food-grade carbon dioxide, meeting relevant specifications, evenly into circulating or still bath water. Guests typically feel fine bubbles clinging to the skin, a warming sensation even when the water is not very hot, and a mildly acidic skin feel. These are experiential phenomena suited to on-site experience design; they are not, in themselves, proof of any medical effect.

Concentration is one of the product’s few quantifiable anchors. Industry communication commonly treats free carbon dioxide of about 1000 ppm or above as the narrative threshold for high concentration. The Japanese reference is 1000 milligrams per kilogram, roughly equivalent to 1000 ppm in a dilute solution, and the figure originates in one of the concentration thresholds used in Japan’s therapeutic-spring classification discussions. The prudent wording is “about 1000 ppm or above, referencing the Japanese therapeutic-spring context”. It should be stated honestly that manufactured bath water is not a hot spring in the sense of Japan’s Hot Spring Act, cannot be called a therapeutic spring, and does not become a hot spring under Chinese regulation merely by reaching this level. Hotels are better equipped with their own testing means and retained sampling records; a measured free-CO2 reading with its time and method noted is more credible than a stack of adjectives.

The boundary with natural springs must be kept clear. A natural carbonated spring comes from a geological source, is scarce and geographically constrained, and is sold on component testing and a place story. An artificial high-concentration carbonated bath comes from equipment, is replicable even for city hotels, and is sold on controllable concentration, visible bubbles and a standardised experience. The two can coexist in one hotel, but only in separate pools, with separate messaging and separate materials. A spring hotel that adds the artificial product must label it as a supplementary artificial experience and must never describe it as “the same natural carbonated spring”. Benefit claims have the same boundary: every experiential description is a non-medical statement, guarantees no individual result and constitutes no treatment advice. Hotel materials should avoid any language promising medical outcomes, and phrases easily read as medical commitments, including “blood circulation promotion”, should be used cautiously in favour of warmth and relaxation language.

It answers four investment tests for hotel differentiation

From an investor’s view, an experience project worth doing should meet four tests at once. Replicable: it does not depend on scarce natural resources and can be standardised across properties. Nameable: it can enter room-type names, booking pages and membership packages. Measurable: key indicators can be tested and recorded, giving claims an evidence base. Pilotable at small scale: a limited trial is allowed before real data sets the pace of further investment. The artificial high-concentration carbonated bath meets all four.

What it offers operations is a set of paths that can be designed and observed, not any revenue promise. First, quality differentiation and pricing logic: in a local market of springless or commoditised business hotels, it adds a photogenic, explainable experience point that supports the value narrative of rooms and packages. Second, room-mix optimisation: private-bath rooms or themed rooms upgrade part of the standard-room inventory into experience supply. Third, repeat visits and reputation: bubbles and the warming feeling lend themselves to review keywords, and the thing to watch is whether guests mention them spontaneously, rather than presetting a positive-rating target. Fourth, seasonal filling: a relaxing overnight-stay theme can be promoted in business low seasons. Fifth, non-room income: private spa rooms, double-bath time slots and experience-zone add-ons create a journey beyond the guest room, subject to actual routing and staffing. These are logical paths, not verified financial conclusions; price gaps and any calculations must return to single-hotel data.

Where to place it: choosing across two hotel types and three scenarios

The first decision that makes or breaks the investment is not the equipment but the first scenario. The scope is limited to three in-hotel settings: guest rooms, the SPA and the swimming pool; public bathhouses are not part of the recommended route.

For city business hotels without a spring, the recommended first phase centres on retrofitted room bathtubs, adding a SPA private room where conditions allow, and preferring a side experience zone over the pool, with whole-pool dissolution not taken as a default first-phase item. Bathtub retrofits are contained changes suited to a few pilot rooms on executive floors or themed floors, with three hard preconditions: bathroom ventilation, concentration and gas-source management, and bathing notice cards. Private-bath rooms can become the hotel’s signature rooms, photogenic and usable in room names and albums, provided waterproofing, drainage, sound insulation and operating procedures are settled first. Private SPA rooms and double baths suit weekend couples and business hospitality; a pure business hotel without a SPA floor can defer this element, because a half-finished experience damages reviews.

For resort hotels that already have hot springs or wellness facilities, the recommended first phase centres on private-bath rooms or SPA private rooms, with a poolside experience zone as a supplement; the main natural-spring pool keeps its original narrative, and the artificial product is always clearly marked as artificial. Rooms and private baths serve as the private option when guests prefer not to use the main pool, or as overflow in bad weather and peak periods, rather than rewriting the genuine-spring story. No material may claim the same effects as a natural carbonated spring.

The pool offers two options. Option A is whole-pool dissolution, considered only after a dedicated assessment covering at least five points: carbon dioxide released from the water surface, indoor air quality and ventilation exchange, compatibility of pH and disinfection systems, the gap between low-temperature body feel and guest expectations, and lifeguarding and opening-hours management. Until the assessment is complete, the pool must not be marketed as a carbonated bath. Option B is a side experience zone using an independent small pool or experience tank whose circulation and concentration are easier to control; it works as a visible photo spot and a light entry point for families and business guests, and is the preferred pool choice for most hotels. Whichever scenario starts first, materials must state the product name, suggested soaking-time range, ventilation notices and contraindication summary, and imagery should prioritise bubble close-ups and concentration notice boards rather than vague adjective posters.

One facility, five guest segments, five entry points

One facility can serve five guest segments at different times and through different channels, with no single segment given priority. High-net-worth silver-age wellness guests value privacy, a slow pace and clear safety cues; they fit private-bath rooms and SPA rooms and are reached through wellness media, offline communities and institutions, and post-check-up interest outreach positioned as lifestyle interest rather than diagnosis or treatment. Affluent lifestyle consumers pay for ritual, shareability and distinctive experiences; they fit SPA rooms, scenic baths and themed suites through the brand website, premium communities and polished short video. Senior business travellers want quick post-trip relaxation without leaving the room; bathtub retrofits and executive-floor rooms fit, reached through corporate agreements, OTA business filters and butler talking points. Couples seek private double use and a sense of occasion; double baths and private-bath rooms fit, promoted through short video, weekend packages and anniversary themes. High-spending families want relaxed parent-child time with a safe, controllable experience; the side zone is easier to control than the whole pool and is promoted through family OTA packages, local-life channels and member events.

Hospitals, check-up centres and health departments are used only for interest-based outreach: information may reach people focused on lifestyle and relaxation, but there must be no hospital endorsement, doctor endorsement, joint diagnosis or treatment, matching with specific clinical programs, binding check-up reports to effect promises, or any wording implying medical adaptation.

Engineering and operations: the hard conditions that decide success

The equipment side is not tied to any brand, and owners can compare suppliers across five modules. For the gas-dissolving and mixing equipment, look at the ability to hold the agreed concentration range steadily, along with noise and footprint. For gas sources and piping, look at compliant cylinder storage, leak monitoring and replacement routing. For water treatment and circulation, check conflicts with existing disinfection and pH systems. For ventilation and air quality, check air-change rates, alarms or inspection routines. For monitoring, check whether non-specialist staff can run concentration sampling and water-temperature records.

Installation priorities differ by scenario. Room bathtubs start with one or a few pilot rooms, focusing on exhaust ventilation and notice cards. For private-bath rooms, structural waterproofing and drainage come before equipment models, with repair space reserved. SPA rooms work best under booking, which helps concentration control and cleaning turnover. Whole-pool dissolution requires joint assessment across mechanical, electrical, water-treatment, HVAC and safety teams. Side experience zones should use independent circulation first, so they do not weaken the main pool’s water-quality model.

Five actions carry daily operations. Front-desk and butler wording stays fixed on artificial high-concentration carbonated bath, relaxing experience and non-medical positioning. Bathing notice cards state duration, ventilation, contraindications and emergency contact. Daily checks cover concentration sampling, ventilation, gas reserves and water-quality indicators. New staff complete wording and emergency drills before going on duty. Complaint rules are set in advance, with refunds, exchanges or rescheduling never softened with effect-based promises. Contraindication notices must follow local rules and legal review, covering at least post-alcohol bathing, acute illness, cautious use or medical advice for serious cardiopulmonary conditions, no solo bathing for frail or mobility-impaired guests, supervision for children, and medical and hotel-policy guidance for pregnant guests and other special groups.

What public cases can prove, and what they cannot

What public materials can verify is whether the facility exists, whether the company officially presents it as a selling point, and whether the operating model is checkable. Verifiable revenue-gain figures are almost nowhere to be found.

The Japanese business chain Super Hotel lists a high-concentration artificial carbonated spring on its official store pages as an attraction, and some stores reinforce memory with named baths. The lesson worth borrowing is that it puts the facility into booking-decision information rather than hiding it at the back of the facilities page. Japan’s regulations, guest mix and rate structure differ from those in China, however, and no publicly verifiable revenue-gain ratio exists; its public-bath format is industry reference only and is not a recommendation to build public bathhouses in China. City hotels in Taiwan such as Jieshibao pair artificial carbonated spring rooms with floor-level SPA; the lesson is using floor SPA to capture add-on spend and longer stays, while local geography and guest mix prevent the case from being copied into a financial model. Domestic hotels and clubs listed on supplier pages show that comparable facilities exist in China, but these remain supplier leads to be checked on site and through contracts rather than treated as revenue cases. Natural carbonated spring resorts such as Yangzonghai and Shuxin Canyon represent the scarce genuine-spring narrative; the artificial route should not borrow that name but tell its own story of controllable concentration, standardised experience and city availability. In short, borrow the model, not the numbers.

Pilot first, measure later: let single-hotel data make the call

The steadiest route has four steps: scenario selection by marking a cell in the matrix; a small pilot of a few rooms or spa rooms, or one experience zone; recorded observations; then single-hotel calculation and a face-to-face discussion. The pilot should cover only one or two cells over 30 to 60 days, rather than every scenario in the first phase; specific investment and financial calculations are discussed separately afterwards against single-hotel conditions.

The pilot observes without preset numeric targets. Exposure covers facility-page clicks, album dwell time and short-video comment keywords. Conversion covers changes in themed-room booking share, SPA and experience add-on counts, and acceptance of on-site upgrades. Value narrative covers whether guests accept room-type price gaps in actual transactions, again without preset figures. Reputation covers whether reviews and questionnaires spontaneously mention bubbles, warmth and relaxation. Operations covers concentration pass rates, ventilation and gas-source incidents, complaint types and staff execution difficulty. Experience covers open-ended satisfaction, with discomfort and contraindication incidents tracked separately as zero-tolerance items. In rhythm, one week goes to engineering, marketing and rooms jointly selecting the scenario; another week to installation and wording sign-off; then a weekly observation period; and finally a review meeting, with a rooms or SPA manager named as pilot lead submitting only a one-page weekly record.

Non-applicability and stop conditions should be set at the same time. Four situations should be ruled out before investing: rooms where ventilation and gas-source safety cannot be solved; a positioning that expects a “medical wellness benchmark” the moment equipment is installed; a public-bathhouse-first plan without the operating capacity to run it; and hopes of using hospital partnerships for medical endorsement. If the pilot shows no positive incremental transaction, no change in booking choices, higher-than-expected operating costs, or complaints and safety risks that cannot be closed, the project should pause for review rather than receiving more investment simply because money has already been spent.

A facility’s existence does not verify demand or returns. What the artificial high-concentration carbonated bath gives a hotel is not a therapeutic certificate but a replicable tool for experience differentiation: springless city hotels build a signature with it, while spring resorts use it to add privacy and absorb overflow. Pilot first, calculate afterwards, and only discuss scale-up after single-hotel verification. That is the safest sequence for an investor.
